Summary

Hierarchical Clustering

Simplest adaptation: hierarchical k-means

l 1. Partition the dataset into k clusters by k-means.

l 2. For each cluster, further partition it into k clusters by kmeans.

  1. Repeat Step 2 recursively, until we reach a termination condition.

¡ For example, the number of points is below the threshold, or the maximum depth is reached.

AGNES and DIANA

Use distance matrix as clustering criteria.

They do not require the number of clusters k as an input, but need a termination condition.

AGNES (Agglomerative Nesting)

Merge nodes that have the greatest similarity.

¡ Go on in a non-descending fashion.

Eventually all nodes belong to the same cluster.

Dendrogram

Decompose data objects into a several levels of nested partitioning (tree of clusters), called a dendrogram.

A clustering of the data objects is obtained by cutting the dendrogram at the desired level, then each connected component forms a cluster.

DIANA (Divisive Analysis)

Inverse order of AGNES.

Eventually each node forms a cluster on its own.

Extensions to Hierarchical Clustering

Major weakness of agglomerative clustering methods:

l Do not scale well: time complexity of at least O(n2), where n is the number of objects.

Can never undo what was done previously.

Integration of hierarchical with distance-based criteria:

l BIRCH: uses CF-tree and incrementally adjusts the quality of sub-clusters.

l CHAMELEON: hierarchical clustering using dynamic modeling.

BIRCH

BIRCH: Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering Using Hierarchies.

Idea: incrementally construct a clustering feature (CF) tree, a hierarchical data structure for multiphase clustering.

Method

l 1. Scan the database to build an initial in-memory CF tree (a multi-level compression of the data that tries to preserve the inherent clustering structure of the data).

  1. Use an arbitrary clustering algorithm to cluster the leaf nodes of the CF tree.

Strength: it scales linearly; i.e., it finds a good clustering with a single scan and improves the quality with a few additional scans.

Weakness: it handles only numeric data, and is sensitive to the order of the data record.

Clustering feature (𝖢𝖥)=(𝖭,𝖫𝖲,𝖲𝖲)( \mathsf { C F } ) = ( \mathsf { N } , \mathsf { L S } , \mathsf { S S } ) .

N: number of data points.

l LS: linear sum of N points’ coordinates.

SS: squared sum of N points’ coordinates.

¡ CF tree

Non-leaf nodes store sums of the CFs of their children.

Two parameters:

Branching factor B: maximum number of children.

Threshold L: maximum diameter of sub-clusters stored at leaf nodes.

l Diameter: square root of average mean squared distance between all pairs of points in a cluster.

diameter(C)=1|C|(|C|−1)∑x∈C,y∈C(dist(x,y))2. d i a m e t e r (C) = \sqrt {\frac {1}{| C | (| C | - 1)} \sum_ {x \in C , y \in C} (d i s t (x , y)) ^ {2}}.

l LS and SS can be used to efficiently compute diameter (for Euclidean distance).

For each point in the input:

¡ Find the closest leaf entry.

¡ Add the point to the leaf entry and update CF.

¡ If number of children > B or diameter > L, then split leaf, and possibly parents.

Example CF tree

CHAMELEON

A hierarchical clustering algorithm which measures the similarity based on a dynamic model.

l Two clusters are merged only if the interconnectivity and closeness (proximity) between two clusters are high relative to the internal interconnectivity of the clusters and closeness of items within the clusters.

¡ A two-phase graph-based algorithm:

l 1. Use a graph-partitioning algorithm: cluster objects into a large number of relatively small sub-clusters.

l 2. Use an agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithm: find the genuine clusters by repeatedly combining these subclusters.

CHAMELEON

Algorithm framework

CHAMELEON

Good at clustering complex objects.

Density-Based Methods

Clustering based on identifying density-connected points.

Major features

Discover clusters of arbitrary shape.

Handle noise.

One scan of database.

Need density parameters as termination condition.

Notable methods

DBSCAN

OPTICS

Density-Based Methods

¡ Two parameters:

ε: radius of ε-neighborhood.

Density-Based Methods

Density-reachable

A point p is density-reachable from a point q with respect to (ε, MinPts), iff. there is a chain of points 𝗉1,...,𝗉𝗇,𝗉1=𝗊,𝗉𝗇=\mathsf { p } _ { 1 } , . . . , \mathsf { p } _ { \mathsf { n } } , \mathsf { p } _ { 1 } = \mathsf { q } , \mathsf { p } _ { \mathsf { n } } = p such that 𝗉𝗂+1\mathsf { p } _ { \mathsf { i } + 1 } is directly density-reachable from pi.

Density-connected

A point p is density-connected to a point q with respect to (ε, MinPts), iff. there is a point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o with respect to (ε, MinPts).

DBSCAN

DBSCAN: Density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise.

¡ A popular clustering algorithm, only second to k-means.

Given a database D, for each point p ∈ D:

l Retrieve all points density-reachable from p with respect to (ε, MinPts).

l If p is a core point, a cluster is formed by finding the maximal set of density-connected points.

¡ p, q ∈ C, iff. p is density-connected to q in C.

¡ If p ∈ C and q is density-reachable to p, then q ∈ C.

l Each core point is processed only once.

Time complexity

l A misclaim in the original paper and many textbooks: O(nlogn).

l O(nlogn) when d is low (e.g., 2), where d is dimensionality.

l The algorithm runs in O(n2) when d is high, and the problem is Ω(𝗇4/3)\Omega ( \mathsf { n } ^ { 4 / 3 } ) . 28 28

DBSCAN

： Strength

l Can find clusters with an arbitrary shape.

Handle noises.

l Do not need to specify the number of clusters.

l Can be applied to non-numeric data (with a distance measure specific to the target data type).

l Almost order-insensitive to the input, except for the points sitting on the edge of two clusteres.

Weakness

Need to choose appropriate parameters (ε, MinPts).

Not good for regions with varying density.

OPTICS

OPTICS: Ordering Points To Identify the Clustering Structure.

Improved version of DBSCAN.

Detect meaningful clusters in data of varying density.

Points are (linearly) ordered such that spatially closest points become neighbors in the ordering.

Introduce two notions apart from DBSCAN:

l The core distance of p: the minimum ε such that p is a core point.

Reachability distance r(p, q) = max(core distance(q), dist(p, q)

DENCLUE

DENCLUE: DENsity-based CLUstEring.

Use statistical density functions.

The influence function describes the impact of a data point within its neighborhood.

Influence of y on x:

fGaussian(x,y)=e−dist(x,y)22σ2. f _ {G a u s s i a n} (x, y) = e ^ {- \frac {d i s t (x , y) ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}}}.

l Gradient of x in the direction of 𝖷i\mathsf { X } _ { \mathrm { i } } :

∇fGaussianD(x,xi)=∑33|D|(xi−x)⋅e−dist(x,xi)22σ2. \nabla f _ {G a u s s i a n} ^ {D} (x, x _ {i}) = \sum_ {3 3} ^ {| D |} (x _ {i} - x) \cdot e ^ {- \frac {d i s t (x , x _ {i}) ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}}}.

DENCLUE

The overall density of the data space is calculated as the sum of the influence functions of all data points.

Clusters are determined mathematically by identifying density attractors.

l Density attractors are local maximal of the overall density function.

l Center-defined clusters: assign to each density attractor the points density attracted to it.

l Arbitrarily-shaped clusters: merge density attractors that are connected through paths of high density.

DENCLUE

S Strength

Solid mathematical foundation.

l Good for datasets with large amounts of noise.

l Allows a compact mathematical description of arbitrarily shaped clusters in high-dimensional datasets.

l Significantly faster than other density-based methods (e.g., DBSCAN).

Weakness

l Has a large number of parameters.

Grid-Based Methods

Use multi-resolution grid data structure.

Notable methods

STING

l CLIQUE

STING

STING: STatistical INformation Grid.

¡ The spatial area is divided into rectangular cells.

There are several levels of cells corresponding to different levels of resolution.

STING

Each cell at a high level is partitioned into a number of smaller cells in the next lower level.

Statistical information of each cell is calculated and stored beforehand and is used to answer queries.

Parameters of higher-level cells can be easily calculated from parameters of lower-level cell.

Count, mean, sum, min, max

Type of distribution: normal, uniform, etc.

STING

Steps

l Use a top-down approach to answer spatial data queries, which identify clusters.

l Start from a pre-selected layer, typically with a small number of cells.

¡ For each cell in the current level compute the confidence interval.

Remove irrelevant cells from further consideration.

l When finish examining the current layer, proceed to the next lower level.

Repeat this process until the bottom layer is reached.

Strength

l Query-independent, easy to parallelize, incremental update.

l Time complexity: O(K), where K is the number of grid cells at the lowest level.

Weakness

l All the cluster boundaries are either horizontal or vertical, and no diagonal boundary is detected.

CLIQUE

CLIQUE: CLustering In QUEst.

Automatically identify subspaces of a high-dimensional data space that allow better clustering than original space.

Can be considered as both density-based and grid-based.

l It partitions each dimension into the same number of equallength interval.

l It partitions a d-dimensional data space into non-overlapping rectangular units (grid cells).

l A unit is dense if the fraction of total data points contained in the unit exceeds the input model parameter.

l A cluster is a maximal set of connected dense units within a subspace.

CLIQUE

Steps

l Divide each dimension into intervals à a grid.

Find dense grid cells.

l Combine dense cells across dimensions.

Identify clusters

Determine dense units in all subspaces of interests.

¡ Determine connected dense units in all subspaces of interests.

l Generate minimal description for the clusters

¡ Determine maximal regions that cover a cluster of connected dense units for each cluster.

¡ Determine minimal cover for each cluster.

Example

CLIQUE

： Strength

l It automatically finds subspaces of the highest dimensionality such that high density clusters exist in those subspaces.

l It is insensitive to the order of objects in input and does not presume any canonical data distribution.

l It scales linearly with the size of input and has good scalability as the number of dimensions in the data increases.

Weakness

l The accuracy of the clustering result may be degraded at the expense of simplicity of the method.
